<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-supported cases and complied with the A1/A2 pressure-question format, but B's architecture held up slightly better under pressure. B's autonomy-from-existing-refusal-rights analogy and its reframe of the "status quo" as already containing unregulated coercion (secret family withholding, violent suicide) neutralized much of A's coercion narrative, and B's answer to A's toughest question (why won't a safeguard inevitably fall to litigation) offered a real distinguishing mechanism (Canada's Charter-driven jurisprudence vs. Oregon's stable 25-year record) rather than a bare assertion. A's slippery-slope and causation/double-effect arguments were genuinely strong and never fully dismantled, and A's resource-diversion point was effectively neutralized by B early with no real recovery. The decisive late exchange favored B: A's concrete answer to the ALS patient ("palliative sedation to unconsciousness") was exposed in B's closing as substituting a different outcome for the one she actually requested, and A's closing—which needed to answer this—was cut off by the word-limit clip before delivering its final rebuttal, leaving B's last substantive point standing. Both openings/closings suffered format clipping penalties, but A's clipped closing cost more because it silenced A's final rejoinder at the most consequential moment.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing rebuttal that A's offer to the ALS patient ("legally unconscious instead") substitutes someone else's values for her actual autonomous request, landing unanswered because A's closing was clipped before it could respond.</best_rebuttal>
